subcategory: Responsible AI, Human Rights and Safety
oneSentence: Designing tools, content and services so people with different disabilities can use them effectively, safely and with dignity.
plainExplanation:
Accessibility means making sure a digital system can be used by people with different disabilities, including people with visual, hearing, mobility, speech, cognitive or psychosocial disabilities. In AI work, this applies both to the system itself and to what it produces. A chatbot, form, dashboard, image description tool or video summary may all need accessible design.

What goes in includes interface choices, content format, language, audio, colour, timing, navigation and any AI features such as speech recognition or image description. What happens is that designers test whether people can perceive the content, operate the controls, understand what is happening and get help when the system makes mistakes. What comes out should be a service more people can use without extra barriers.

Accessibility is not the same as general inclusion, although they overlap. Inclusion is broader and asks who is welcomed and able to participate. Accessibility is more specific: it asks whether a person can actually use the tool or service in practice. It is also not the same as convenience features for everyone, though some accessible design helps many users.

In AI, accessibility also means checking whether the model creates new barriers. For example, speech recognition may work less well for some accents or speech patterns, automatic captions may miss key words, and image generators may produce visuals without meaningful text alternatives. Because of that, human review and testing with disabled users remain important.

everydayAnalogy.title: A public meeting with many ways to participate
everydayAnalogy.story: A town hall in Nairobi invites residents to comment on a new transport plan. At the entrance, there is a ramp as well as stairs, the agenda is available in large print, the speaker uses a microphone, and questions can be asked by voice or by writing on cards. More people can take part because the organisers changed the setup, not the people. The goal is not to give special treatment; it is to remove barriers that the original setup created.

mapping.aiElement: Accessible design choices such as keyboard access, readable text and captions

mapping.analogyElement: Questions accepted in more than one way
mapping.aiElement: Multiple input and output options, such as text, speech and screen-reader support
Developers and organisations being responsible for reducing barriers

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A meeting room is a physical place, while many accessibility issues in AI are dynamic and depend on software behaviour. For example, an AI system can produce inaccessible outputs, such as poor captions or unlabeled images, even if the basic interface is well designed. The analogy also does not show that accessibility needs ongoing testing with real users, not just one-time setup.

visual.title: Checking accessibility in an AI-supported service
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to describe accessibility as a step-by-step design and review process, not a last-minute add-on.
visual.description: A left-to-right sequence of five boxes shows how an AI-supported service becomes more accessible. Read from identifying users and barriers, to designing choices, testing, fixing problems and reviewing outputs in real use. Each step names one action and one result.

steps.label: 1. Identify users and barriers
steps.explanation: List who may use the service, including people with different disabilities, and note likely barriers such as unreadable text, audio-only information or time limits.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with small icons for text, audio, keyboard and screen reader. Add a caption line: 'Who might be blocked and why?'

steps.label: 2. Design multiple ways to use it
steps.explanation: Provide more than one way to perceive and operate the service, such as captions, keyboard navigation, clear language and text alternatives for images.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box with parallel paths labelled 'see', 'hear', 'type', 'navigate'. Connect from step 1 with an arrow.

steps.label: 3. Test with assistive tools and people
steps.explanation: Check the service with tools like screen readers and keyboard-only navigation, and if possible with disabled users, because design assumptions often miss real barriers.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box with a magnifying glass over a web page and small labels 'screen reader', 'keyboard', 'user test'.

steps.label: 4. Fix both interface and AI output
steps.explanation: Correct barriers in the layout and in AI-generated results, such as inaccurate captions, confusing summaries or images without useful descriptions.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth box split in two halves: 'interface' and 'AI output', each with a repair icon.

steps.label: 5. Monitor and improve
steps.explanation: Keep reviewing complaints, errors and changing user needs, because accessibility can break when content, models or workflows change.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fifth box with a feedback loop arrow returning to step 1 and a small note icon for reports.

visual.interaction: On hover or focus, each step reveals one example barrier and one example fix. Keyboard users can move step by step with tab and arrow keys.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is an ordered process with five steps. First, identify who may use the service and what might block them, including barriers related to vision, hearing, mobility, cognition or time pressure. Second, design more than one way to access content and controls. Third, test with assistive technologies and, where possible, disabled users. Fourth, fix problems in both the interface and the AI outputs. Fifth, keep monitoring and improving because new content or model changes can create new barriers. The main point is that accessibility is continuous work across design, testing and operation.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static horizontal row of five numbered boxes with arrows between them shows the same sequence. The final box includes a dashed arrow back to the first box to show ongoing improvement without animation.

workedExample.scenario: A team uses an AI tool to group 240 survey comments about problems at a public clinic.
workedExample.input: Comments arrive in plain text, voice notes and photos of handwritten forms.
process: The team converts voice notes to text, but keeps human checks because automatic transcription may mishear some speakers.
They add text alternatives for the photos and make sure the review screen works with keyboard-only navigation and screen readers.
They ask two staff members to test the tool: one uses a screen reader and one enlarges text to 200 percent.
Testing shows the colour-only category labels are hard to distinguish and some AI summaries drop important details from short comments.
The team changes the labels to include text, improves contrast, and requires human review before any grouped summary is shared.
workedExample.result: More staff can use the tool, and the final grouped report keeps issues that might otherwise have been missed, such as repeated complaints about inaccessible entrances and long waiting times.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: After a disaster, a UN team uses AI-assisted analysis on satellite imagery to help create public situation updates and internal planning materials. Accessibility means the dashboards, maps and summaries should be usable by staff with different disabilities, and public-facing outputs should include readable text, clear structure and alternatives for image-heavy content.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: If accessibility is ignored, useful evidence may not reach all staff who need it, and affected people may receive updates in formats they cannot use. Accessible design improves participation, review quality and accountability.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place protection-sensitive, personal or security-sensitive information into an unapproved public AI service. Human review is still needed before sharing image-based findings, because AI outputs can be incomplete or misleading.

whyItMatters: Accessibility affects who can participate, who is excluded and whose needs are overlooked. For a non-specialist, this matters because an AI tool can appear efficient while quietly blocking colleagues, applicants, service users or members of the public. That can lead to weaker evidence, unfair outcomes, legal and human rights risks, and avoidable safety problems. Accessibility also improves decision-making quality: when more people can use a system and check its outputs, errors are more likely to be found. In practice, it shifts the question from 'Can the tool run?' to 'Can people with different abilities actually use it and challenge it?'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accessibility only matters for a small group of users.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Many people benefit from accessible design, including people with permanent disabilities, temporary injuries, low bandwidth, noisy environments, ageing-related changes or limited digital skills. Even when the core purpose is disability access, the practical benefit often reaches much wider.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an interface meets a checklist, the AI service is accessible.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Checklists help, but they do not guarantee that the whole service works. An AI system can still create inaccessible outputs, such as poor captions, confusing summaries or unlabeled images. Real testing with assistive technology and users is needed to catch those problems.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accessibility is the same as inclusion.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They overlap, but they are not identical. Inclusion asks who is able to participate and feels welcomed. Accessibility focuses more narrowly on whether people can perceive, operate and understand the service in practice. A project may talk about inclusion while still leaving concrete barriers in place.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Make the tool usable by people with different disabilities, not just by the average user.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Accessibility in digital systems means designing and maintaining interfaces and outputs so users with disabilities can perceive information, operate controls, understand interactions and complete tasks with appropriate assistive technologies and alternative modes. In AI systems, this covers both the front-end experience and the model-produced content, such as captions, summaries, image descriptions, recommendations or conversational replies. Relevant checks may include keyboard operability, screen-reader compatibility, colour contrast, clear structure, text alternatives, caption quality, timing controls, error recovery and usability testing with disabled people. Accessibility is related to inclusion and non-discrimination, but it is not identical to either: it focuses on practical barriers in use.

keyTakeaway: Accessibility means removing barriers so people with different disabilities can actually use the system and its outputs, not just be counted as potential users.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows accessibility in an AI-supported service?
options: A team adds a chatbot but offers only audio replies because it feels modern.
A dashboard uses colour alone to mark risk levels and assumes everyone can see them clearly.
A service provides captions, keyboard navigation, clear headings and human review of AI-generated image descriptions.
An organisation says it values inclusion but does not test whether disabled users can complete key tasks.
quickCheck.explanation: The third option removes practical barriers in both the interface and the AI output. Accessibility is about whether people can use the service in reality, not just whether the organisation has good intentions or modern features.
